reachable: Yes, at the scored position. The tie constrains addr_src.weight / addr_dst.weight, which the r23 arch uses at EVERY command position: a_h = GELU(addr_in(LN(cmd_raw))), a_src = unit(addr_src(a_h)), a_dst = unit(addr_dst(a_h)); a_src reads the transport store at that step, the read becomes the pointer query, and the blend goes into pred at command positions through tp_out, masked only by valid_cmd (not by observation presence). So the read command's own prediction depends on the tied weights whether or not its observation is withheld. Gradient in training: the address heads receive gradient only through the zero-init (D,D) tp_out gate, which the author states explicitly as the motivation for the mechanism; it is nonzero once tp_out moves off zero. Confirmed empirically that the pair moves and that the tie holds it on the manifold under real gradient pressure (mean |cos| 0.10 at init -> 0.97 by step 20 -> 0.999 late). The tail average likewise acts on the weights that are then measured: the adapter scores the net returned by H._train, and commit fires on the last of exactly `steps` opt.step() calls (harness loops `for step in range(1, steps+1)`).
solves_outside_model: No. The module imports only `math` and `torch`. `make(params, steps, **p)` receives bare parameter tensors and an int; the impl never sees a batch, a token, a target, the data root, a file, or an environment variable, and it registers no hooks. Both mechanisms are post-step operations on weight tensors, identical at training and scoring positions. There is no path by which resolved move-chain routing could reach the model's input — no command is parsed anywhere in the file. This is the cleanest possible shape with respect to the prior retraction.
summary: The code does what the hypothesis says. Mechanism 1 (role tie): I verified by execution that the closed-form 2x2 Gram diagonalisation reproduces the exact best column-wise rank-one factorisation — max deviation from torch.linalg.svd is 4.6e-7 — that it is symmetric under swapping the pair (2.4e-7), that all degenerate branches (both columns zero, either zero, orthogonal columns) stay finite and pick the right direction, and that on the actual genome the shape rule selects exactly (addr_src.weight, addr_dst.weight) and nothing else. Repeated lam=0.15 pulls drive the pair to collinearity in a few tens of steps as claimed, and the constraint holds under real gradient pressure (mean |cos| 0.999 late in training). Mechanism 2 (tail average): _TailAverage reproduces a reference bias-corrected EMA exactly (max diff 0.0), commits once at the final step, is idempotent, and demonstrably changes the returned weights relative to the last iterate; the LR floor is 0.20 of base at the end versus the parent's 0.05, with warmup 0.04 and hold 0.30 unchanged, all verified against the parent source. Muon and spectral-cap membership are byte-for-byte the parent's behaviour on this genome (Muon on the (64,192)x8 and (64,256)x2 groups; cap on tr_read/x_out/tp_out). The net has LayerNorm only and zero buffers, so the "averaged weights need no recalibration" argument is correct. Cost measured at ~5% per-step overhead on CPU and a 21.9 MB fp32 shadow. No fabricated measurements: the only run-derived number in the hypothesis is a pure-Python brute-force check of the projector, which is executable without torch and which my torch-side SVD comparison independently corroborates, and n=89 comes from the BRIEF. The author explicitly labels everything else UNMEASURED. Three minor imprecisions, none behavioural: a miscounted trunk shape group, "re-applies the tie" being one 15% pull rather than a projection, and an EMA framed as a 45-100% uniform tail average. WHAT I COULD NOT CHECK: whether the mechanism actually raises comp_ca — no data root here, the eval is noisy (floor 0.0227), and a synthetic-gradient loop says nothing about the real objective; also untested on GPU/bf16, though the tie casts to float32 internally and copies back through .to(u.dtype), so it is dtype-safe by construction.

divergences.claim: "the [64,192] group inherited from the r18 trunk has six members and is left alone"
divergences.what_the_code_does: The (64,192) group on this genome has EIGHT members (file_read, file_write, path_read, path_write, sys_val, tr_path, xq, xk), and they come from the r22 prefix-xattention base, not an r18 trunk. Behaviourally identical — any count != 2 is inert for the tie, and all eight still route to Muon exactly as in the parent.
divergences.evidence: Built the genome's net + r18 head and enumerated 2-D params: (64,192)x8, (64,256)x2, (64,768)x2, (768,768)x3. Instantiating the optimizer gives opt.tie.pairs == [(addr_src.weight, addr_dst.weight)] only.

divergences.claim: "at the final optimizer step writes the average back ... then re-applies the role tie and the spectral cap, so the returned weights sit on the same constraints the trajectory did"
divergences.what_the_code_does: The post-commit tie call is `self.tie.project(self.total)`, which is a single lam=0.15 INTERPOLATION toward the rank-one factorisation, not a projection onto it. The averaged weights therefore sit slightly off the manifold the trajectory sat on. Measured on a 200-step synthetic run: trajectory last iterate mean|cos| 0.99991, raw EMA 0.99976, after the single re-tie pull 0.99982. The residual is tiny, so the overstatement has no practical consequence here, but "sit on the same constraints" is stronger than what runs.
divergences.evidence: /private/tmp/rev25/t5.py — intercepted the final step, committed the EMA, and measured collinearity before and after the re-tie pull.

divergences.claim: "From 45% of the step budget onward the impl accumulates a bias-corrected exponential moving average ... with horizon 12% of the budget" framed in the falsification section as an average over "45%-100% of the budget"
divergences.what_the_code_does: The code is exactly what the first sentence says — decay = 1 - 1/(0.12*steps), accumulation gated at step >= 0.45*steps, bias-corrected by 1-decay^count. But because the horizon is 12% of the budget, the EMA weight on the iterate at 45% is exp(-0.55/0.12) ~ 1%, so the effective averaging window is the last ~12-25%, not 45-100%. The horizon is stated explicitly, so nothing is hidden; the 45%-100% framing in failure-mode 3 just describes a wider window than the estimator actually has. Calling an EMA "Polyak-Ruppert tail averaging / SWA" is likewise a loose label (both are uniform averages), though the text says "exponential moving average" outright.
divergences.evidence: _TailAverage verified against a hand-written bias-corrected EMA: max diff 0.0 (/private/tmp/rev25/t3.py). decay computed as 0.857 for steps=60 (horizon 7).
